Shanghai/Ningbo.note: Both ports have been open since 28 August; what remains is queue, not closure. The queue is finally coming down, but slowly and from a very high peak. Linerlytica's 6 September snapshot puts 1.41M TEU on 239 ships at anchorage off Shanghai/Ningbo, down from the 1.84M TEU peak on 31 August and from 1.58M on 4 September. That is roughly back to the 24 August pre-Saudel level of 1.42M. The queue-to-berth ratio tells a less comfortable story: 2.92, versus 2.66 on 24 August and 3.02 on 4 September, and it ticked UP from 2.63 on 5 September. Every other tracked port sits between 0.13 and 1.17. So the backlog is roughly six times the next-worst port and has not cleared. No terminal-level waiting time has been published anywhere since SEKO's 4 September update, so the 5-9 day range here is four days old and should be read as such rather than as a current measurement. Krovanh itself is no longer a factor for these ports — it has weakened to a tropical depression 1,117 km away and is tracking toward Japan; it leads the event name only because it is the system still active in the JMA feed while the Saudel backlog works off.

remarks: One active tropical cyclone worldwide and it threatens nothing we track. Krovanh has been downgraded to a tropical depression at 26.0N 132.0E, 1,051 km from Busan at its closest approach to any tracked port — well beyond the 600 km threshold, and moving further away.

Shanghai/Ningbo is the only port carrying a weather entry. It is open and recovering, not closed. Anchorage volume is down 23% from the 31 August peak, but the queue-to-berth ratio of 2.92 is still about six times the next-worst tracked port.
No new closures. Qingdao, Busan, Shenzhen (Yantian) and Xiamen are all operating normally with queue ratios between 0.32 and 0.63.

Source freshness warning: SEKO has not updated its page since 4 September and Kuehne+Nagel's weekly port update is unavailable. The waiting-time figures shown are the 4 September ones, carried forward unchanged rather than re-measured.
New York's queue-to-berth ratio fell from 3.33 to 0.82 between 5 and 6 September and Norfolk's from 1.14 to 0.33. Neither is weather-driven — both look like a berthing backlog clearing.
